It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.

transcript.text:
Greyhollow clings to the slope of the mountains the townsfolk call the Reach, high above the tree line, where the wind never quite stops. Everything in the town lives off the mine, and the mine was good to them — until three days ago.

Brakka Ironvein knows this spot as well as anyone. For six years he kept watch at the Temple of the Anvil Father, the god of forge and pick, and he has stood before this same tunnel on colder nights than this. But tonight is different. The old north workings, sealed a generation ago, have swallowed three miners, and last night they spat back a fourth man who babbled of lights that walk and was dead by dawn.

Now it is late afternoon, and the sun has already slipped behind the peaks. The mouth of the mine yawns black before him. Hessa, the old prior, pressed the temple's hooded lantern into his hand and gave him one charge: go down before sunrise, and bring back whoever can still be brought back. At dawn the council means to brick this entrance shut, missing miners or not.

The lantern hangs unlit from his fist. The tunnel mouth waits.

I check my gear first: shield strapped tight, sword loose in its scabbard. Then I light Hessa's lantern and step into the tunnel, keeping an eye out for fresh boot prints or dropped tools near the entrance, anything that shows where the three miners went.

He straps the shield tight, eases the sword in its scabbard, and works the lantern's shutter open. A spark from the tinderbox catches the wick, and warm light spills down the tunnel: a broad, timber-framed gallery running straight into the mountain, rusted rails for the ore carts set into the floor. The place smells of cold stone and old coal dust.

The floor near the mouth is a churn of footprints, trampled flat by the search parties who have been in and out for three days, and he cannot pick the three miners' boots out of that crowd. Farther in, though, where the trampling thins, one set of prints shows clearer than the rest: a single man's boots, scuffed and uneven, the strides sometimes long, sometimes dragging, leading back toward the entrance — the fourth man's last walk up out of the dark.

Beyond the reach of the light, the gallery runs on into blackness and splits.

I follow the fourth man's trail backward into the mine, holding the lantern high and my shield ready, watching for any blood or dropped gear along the way. When I reach the split, I'll check which branch his prints come from.

Lantern held high, shield ready, he walks backward down the fourth man's trail, away from the mouth. The gallery slopes gently downward, its timber props leaning with age, and the clean print of one boot after another leads him on.

It does not take long to see the man did not come up whole. Dark drops lie on the stone floor, dried to black — scattered at first, then more steadily — and there is a handprint smeared on the wall at shoulder height, where he paused to lean. A little farther on, a miner's pick lies where it was dropped, its haft smeared dark.

The trail carries him to the split. The right-hand branch climbs slightly, its rails bright with use: the active workings. The left-hand branch runs level a way and then down into older, darker timbers, and it is from there that the bloody boot prints come, one dragging stride after another.

I pick up the bloodied pick to look it over for anything odd, then take the left branch, following the prints deeper into the older timbers. I keep the lantern high and my shield ready, and I'll stop to listen every few dozen paces.

The pick is plain iron and ash, its head worn smooth by years of work. The dark smear is blood, dried and flaking, left where a torn hand last gripped it — the same hand as the print on the wall. Nothing else is odd about it.

He takes the left branch and follows the prints down. The timbers grow older and more crooked, the rails long rusted away to red powder, and the air turns cold and stale, with no movement in it but his own. Each time he halts to listen, the silence closes in around him, heavy as water. Once or twice he catches something: far ahead, faint and irregular, a dry scrape, like something heavy dragged over stone — and then it stops, as if whatever makes it is listening too.

The tunnel ends at a wall of fitted stone and squared timber: the old seal across the north workings. It has been broken open, a rough hole knocked through near the floor, its edges snapped inward. The bloody boot prints pass straight through it into the dark.

I crouch at the hole and check how the seal was broken: were the timbers smashed from outside or pushed from within? I'll shutter the lantern halfway, listen a moment, then squeeze through shield first with my sword drawn.

Kneeling at the hole, he reads the break the way he would read a cracked seam in stone. The seal was not smashed from this side. The splinters of timber and the chips of stone lie scattered on the mine side of the wall, and the fractures in the blocks run from the workings outward. Whatever opened this hole came through from within — and the break is fresh, the raw wood pale and the stone dust still bright, no more than a few days old.

He lowers the lantern's hood until only a dim circle of light clings to his feet, and holds still. In the silence he hears it plainly now: the scrape, a dragging rhythm somewhere far down the workings — and beneath it a thread of sound that makes his breath catch. A man's voice, low and hoarse, too far off for the words, rising and falling like someone muttering to himself. It comes from ahead and to the left.

Then he works himself through the hole, shield first, sword already drawn, and comes up on the far side into air that is cold and old and still, into a darkness that drinks the little light.

I stay low and still just inside the breach, let my eyes adjust, then open the lantern shutter a crack to see what lies around me. If the way is clear, I creep toward that muttering voice, ahead and to the left, keeping my shield up and my steps quiet.

On the far side, the old workings open into a low, broad gallery. His dwarf eyes, long at home in the dark, pick out the shapes even before the lantern: squared timbers leaning like tired old men, a rusted ore cart tipped on its side, a thick drift of black dust that has lain undisturbed for a generation. The lantern's cracked shutter throws only a thin sliver of light ahead of him.

He moves quietly, the mail muffled under his steady tread, shield up, sword ready, and follows the voice. Step by step it resolves out of the dark — a man's voice, cracked and dry, repeating the same words over and over like a man too tired to stop talking: "...don't follow the light... don't follow the light..."

And then, at the far end of the gallery where it bends, he sees it. A pale light, greenish-white and cold, drifting slowly in the air — no lamp, no flame, just a hovering glow that bobs a little as it moves. The voice comes from somewhere just beyond it.

I stop and stay in the shadow of a leaning timber, shutter the lantern fully, and watch the light for a moment to see how it moves and whether it is drawn to anything. Then I whisper toward the voice, low and steady: "Friend, I'm from Greyhollow, sent by Prior Hessa. Are you one of the miners?" I keep my shield up and don't step toward the light.

He shuts the lantern down to nothing and lets the dark take him. His dwarf eyes make the gallery out in gray, and against it the pale light stands out like a cold star. He watches it a long moment: it does not drift aimlessly. It circles, slow and patient as a fish, around something just past the bend — bobbing, dimming, brightening again — and it pays his stillness no mind. It is not drawn to him. It is waiting on something.

His whisper goes out into the silence. The muttering stops. For a heartbeat there is nothing, and then a voice comes back, hoarse and cracked and almost disbelieving.

"Greyhollow? Hessa sent you?" A wet cough. "Anvil Father be praised. Name's Durn. Durn Rask. There were three of us." Another cough, and something like a sob pushed down. "The others are gone — it led them off, one by one, down the old drift. Don't follow it, friend, whatever it shows you. It's been circling me three days, waiting."

As Durn speaks, the light goes still. Then it drifts a little way toward the sound of Brakka's voice, brightening as it comes, and stops just short of the bend, hovering there like it is listening.

"Easy, Durn. I'm Brakka Ironvein, and I'm coming to get you out. Can you walk, and is there anything between you and me besides that light?" I keep my shield up and my eyes off the glow, watching the floor and Durn's voice instead, and I wait for his answer before I move.

"I called down till I had no voice left," Durn says quietly. "There was a moan, once, right after — then nothing. That's three days gone. No man lives at the bottom of a winze that long. Arris and Keld are gone."

The pick rings dull against the center of the floor — hollow, ready to go. Near the bend the floor is already gone, a ragged black mouth in the stone where the old winze drops away out of sight. Along the left wall the stone sounds truer under the pick, and the timber props stand closer together there, but the wood is old and powder-white, and Brakka cannot be certain it will bear his weight in mail. It is the only way forward, though: the hole spans the middle of the gallery, and Durn lies against the far wall, just past the bend, on the other side of it.

Over the mouth of the winze the pale light hangs, patient as ever, brightening and dimming like slow breath.

"I'm sorry about Arris and Keld, Durn. Hold on, I'm coming to you." I take the lantern off my belt and loop the rope or strap if I have one around the sturdiest timber prop for a tether; if not, I test each prop with the pick before I trust it, then ease along the left wall one step at a time with my shield on my back and my free hand on the stone, eyes never on the light.

The tether is set — the rope looped around the stoutest of the old timbers and drawn snug. He shrugs the shield onto his back, sets his free hand to the cold stone, and steps out along the wall, keeping his eyes on the rock and the floor and anything at all but the light.

He has gone perhaps ten careful paces when the floor lies to him. A timber groans, the stone under his foot crumbles like old biscuit, and the world drops out from beneath him. The rope snaps taut with a violence that slams him into the wall and drives the breath from his chest. He hangs, spinning slowly, over the black mouth of the winze, the rope biting the prop above him.

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. story.text:
# Story so far

## Setup
- World: Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside of the Reach (the mountains above the tree line). Everything in town lives off the mine.
- Date/time at game start: the 14th of Frost, 841, late afternoon (set to 5:00 PM).
- Brakka Ironvein: hill dwarf fighter 1, acolyte of the Anvil Father. Served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow. STR 15, CON 16, WIS 14, AC 18 (chain mail 16 + shield 2), 14 HP, Second Wind 1/1, 15 gp, borrowed hooded lantern, 50 ft hempen rope, miner's pick (gained later).
- Crisis: three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings (sealed a generation ago, ~50 years) and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up alone babbling about "lights that walk," then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow (the 15th of Frost, sunrise), missing miners or not. Prior Hessa (old dwarf) asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. This is the quest "Bring back the miners" (open).

## What happened (turn by turn)

Turn 1: Brakka checked gear, lit the borrowed lantern (6-hour timer started), stepped into the mine. Perception 11: floor near mouth churned by search parties; couldn't pick out the three miners' prints. Farther in, found one fresher set — a single man's uneven, dragging prints leading back toward the entrance (the fourth man's last walk up). Gallery is timber-framed, rusted ore-cart rails.

Turn 2: Followed the fourth man's trail backward into the mine (Perception 18). Found dark dried blood drops on the floor, a handprint smear on the wall at shoulder height, and a dropped miner's pick with blood-smeared haft. Reached a split: right branch climbs (active workings, bright rails); left branch runs level then down into older, darker timbers — the bloody prints come from there.

Turn 3: Picked up the bloodied miner's pick (now carried; ordinary iron and ash, worn, blood where a torn hand gripped it). Took the left branch. Listening (Perception 17): heard a faint, irregular dry scrape far ahead, like something heavy dragged over stone, that stopped when he stopped. Reached the seal across the north workings: fitted stone and squared timber, breached by a rough hole knocked through near the floor, edges snapped inward.

Turn 4: Crouched at the hole. Stonecunning check (INT History, 1d20+3 = 22): the seal was NOT smashed from the mine side — splinters and chips lie on the mine side, fractures run from the workings outward. Whatever opened it came through from within, and the break is fresh (raw wood pale, stone dust bright), a few days old at most. He lowered the lantern hood and listened (natural 20 Perception, 24): heard the scrape clearly, plus beneath it a man's voice, low and hoarse, muttering, from ahead and to the left. He squeezed through shield-first, sword drawn.

Turn 5: Crept through the old workings (Stealth with disadvantage from chain mail, rolled 19). Reached a low broad gallery: leaning timbers, a tipped rusted ore cart, black dust. The muttering resolved into words: "...don't follow the light... don't follow the light..." At the far end where the gallery bends, saw a pale greenish-white light, hovering, bobbing, no lamp or flame.

Turn 6: Stopped in shadow, shuttered the lantern fully, whispered: "Friend, I'm from Greyhollow, sent by Prior Hessa. Are you one of the miners?" The muttering stopped; a hoarse voice answered: "Greyhollow? Hessa sent you? ... Name's Durn. Durn Rask. There were three of us. ... The others are gone — it led them off, one by one, down the old drift. Don't follow it, friend, whatever it shows you. It's been circling me three days, waiting." As Durn spoke, the light stilled, then drifted a little toward Brakka's voice, brightening, stopping just short of the bend.

Turn 7: Brakka: "Easy, Durn. I'm Brakka Ironvein, and I'm coming to get you out. Can you walk...?" Durn answered: can't walk, left leg broken. The light showed them a silver seam "bright as running water" down an unmapped drift; the floor gave way under Arris; Durn went for him and it gave way under Durn too. There's a hole past the bend, a straight drop — the old winze. Arris and Keld are at the bottom of it. Durn caught a timber and dragged himself back. Warned: don't trust the floor, don't watch the light, it shows you things you want.

Turn 8: Brakka asked if Arris and Keld are alive down there, tested the floor with the pick butt (Survival 10), looked for a safe path along the wall. Durn: called down until he had no voice; there was a moan once, right after, then nothing — three days ago; no man lives at the bottom of a winze that long. Arris and Keld are gone. Floor test: the center of the floor sounds hollow; near the bend it's already gone (a ragged black mouth — the winze). Along the left wall the stone sounds truer and timbers stand closer, but the wood is old and powder-white, uncertain under his armored weight. The hole spans the middle of the gallery; Durn lies against the far wall just past the bend, on the other side. The pale light hangs over the winze mouth.

## Where things stand at end of turn 8 (before turn 9's crossing attempt)

- Brakka is in the north workings, before the bend, near the timber prop. He has the rope in hand (50 ft), shield still on, sword ready. Durn is past the bend, beyond the winze, against the far wall, broken leg, been there three days. The wisp hovers over the winze mouth, between them.
- The winze is an unmapped deep shaft past the bend; Arris and Keld fell in and are dead (silence for three days). The drift dead-ends behind Durn (a blind pocket — the miners were lured into a dead end, then the floor collapsed).

## Decisions made (some not yet revealed in play)

- The "walking light" is a will-o'-wisp (SRD Will-o'-Wisp, CR 2). It haunts the north workings; it is what the fourth man called "lights that walk." It lured the miners to their deaths and has been circling the dying Durn, waiting to feed (Consume Life).
- The wisp mimics the voices of the dead to lure the living toward the winze.
- The breach in the seal was forced from within the workings (something pushed out toward the mine), and is recent (a few days).
- Durn's companions: Arris and Keld, both dead at the bottom of the winze.

## Notebook entries and key facts
- Brakka Ironvein (person); Greyhollow (place); the Reach (place); the mine (place); the north workings (place, sealed a generation ago, now breached); Temple of the Anvil Father (place, inside Greyhollow); the Anvil Father (god, patron of forge and pick); Hessa (person, prior); the three missing miners (group: two dead, Durn survives); the fourth man (person, died before dawn); the town council (group, will brick up the mine at sunrise tomorrow); Durn Rask (person, surviving miner, broken leg); Arris (person, dead); Keld (person, dead); the old winze (place, inside the north workings, where Arris and Keld fell); the walking light (creature, a will-o'-wisp).
- Places linked: Temple of the Anvil Father inside Greyhollow; the mine adjoining Greyhollow; the north workings inside the mine; the old winze inside the north workings; Greyhollow inside the Reach.
- Timeline: north workings sealed ~50 years ago; miners disappeared 3 days ago (11th of Frost); fourth man came up and died yesterday (13th of Frost); council will brick up the entrance at sunrise tomorrow (15th of Frost).
- Quest "Bring back the miners" (open): bring back whoever can still be brought back before sunrise; the council will seal the entrance at sunrise; a hoarse voice was heard (Durn).

## Open threads / plans
- Brakka intends to reach Durn, get him out before sunrise tomorrow, and escape the mine. The wisp stands between them and is hostile.
- The silver seam in the winze (revealed by the wisp's lure) may or may not be real — not yet confirmed in play. (I later decided in turn 13, not yet in play at this point, that it IS real — see below.)

## State carried into the future (things decided that matter)
- The wisp is the central threat and is hostile; it fights as a skirmisher (fly 50 ft, hover; Shock +4 to hit, 2d8 lightning; AC 19, HP 22; resists nonmagical weapon damage; can turn invisible as an action, which requires concentration; Consume Life targets a 0-HP creature within 5 ft, DC 10 Con save or die, heals the wisp 3d6 on a kill).
- This is a deadly fight for a solo level 1 character (CR 2). Planned resolution direction: the wisp need not be defeated in a slugfest — it is a lurer/skirmisher and may disengage and flee if Brakka resists or hurts it; and the "turning points" rule (owner's wish) may come into play if Brakka does something heroic or true to his faith (raising the holy symbol, shielding Durn) at a true climax, with no mechanical benefit — the Anvil Father answers, and the wisp recoils/flees. Not yet used.
- From turn 13 onward (already in play): the fallen beam is rotten through; the winze narrows to a ~5-foot gap at the bend (jumpable with a run); and the silver seam in the winze's walls is REAL (the wisp showed the miners truth, and used it to lure them).

## Exact words that may matter again
- Durn's warning, repeated: "...don't follow the light... don't follow the light..." and "Don't trust the floor, and don't watch the light. It shows you things you want."
- The wisp's lure-voice in the shaft: "Brakka... help me... I'm still down here... don't leave me like the others..." (Durn: "That weren't my voice. Don't listen to it.")

- World: Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside of the Reach (the mountains above the tree line). Everything in town lives off the mine.

- Crisis: three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings (sealed a generation ago, ~50 years) and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up alone babbling about "lights that walk," then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow (the 15th of Frost, sunrise), missing miners or not. Prior Hessa (old dwarf) asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. This is the quest "Bring back the miners" (open).

## What happened (turn by turn)

Turn 1: Brakka checked gear, lit the borrowed lantern (6-hour timer started), stepped into the mine. Perception 11: floor near mouth churned by search parties; couldn't pick out the three miners' prints. Farther in, found one fresher set — a single man's uneven, dragging prints leading back toward the entrance (the fourth man's last walk up). Gallery is timber-framed, rusted ore-cart rails.

Turn 2: Followed the fourth man's trail backward into the mine (Perception 18). Found dark dried blood drops on the floor, a handprint smear on the wall at shoulder height, and a dropped miner's pick with blood-smeared haft. Reached a split: right branch climbs (active workings, bright rails); left branch runs level then down into older, darker timbers — the bloody prints come from there.

Turn 3: Picked up the bloodied miner's pick (now carried; ordinary iron and ash, worn, blood where a torn hand gripped it). Took the left branch. Listening (Perception 17): heard a faint, irregular dry scrape far ahead, like something heavy dragged over stone, that stopped when he stopped. Reached the seal across the north workings: fitted stone and squared timber, breached by a rough hole knocked through near the floor, edges snapped inward.

Turn 4: Crouched at the hole. Stonecunning check (INT History, 1d20+3 = 22): the seal was NOT smashed from the mine side — splinters and chips lie on the mine side, fractures run from the workings outward. Whatever opened it came through from within, and the break is fresh (raw wood pale, stone dust bright), a few days old at most. He lowered the lantern hood and listened (natural 20 Perception, 24): heard the scrape clearly, plus beneath it a man's voice, low and hoarse, muttering, from ahead and to the left. He squeezed through shield-first, sword drawn.

Turn 5: Crept through the old workings (Stealth with disadvantage from chain mail, rolled 19). Reached a low broad gallery: leaning timbers, a tipped rusted ore cart, black dust. The muttering resolved into words: "...don't follow the light... don't follow the light..." At the far end where the gallery bends, saw a pale greenish-white light, hovering, bobbing, no lamp or flame.

Turn 6: Stopped in shadow, shuttered the lantern fully, whispered: "Friend, I'm from Greyhollow, sent by Prior Hessa. Are you one of the miners?" The muttering stopped; a hoarse voice answered: "Greyhollow? Hessa sent you? ... Name's Durn. Durn Rask. There were three of us. ... The others are gone — it led them off, one by one, down the old drift. Don't follow it, friend, whatever it shows you. It's been circling me three days, waiting." As Durn spoke, the light stilled, then drifted a little toward Brakka's voice, brightening, stopping just short of the bend.

Turn 7: Brakka: "Easy, Durn. I'm Brakka Ironvein, and I'm coming to get you out. Can you walk...?" Durn answered: can't walk, left leg broken. The light showed them a silver seam "bright as running water" down an unmapped drift; the floor gave way under Arris; Durn went for him and it gave way under Durn too. There's a hole past the bend, a straight drop — the old winze. Arris and Keld are at the bottom of it. Durn caught a timber and dragged himself back. Warned: don't trust the floor, don't watch the light, it shows you things you want.

Turn 8: Brakka asked if Arris and Keld are alive down there, tested the floor with the pick butt (Survival 10), looked for a safe path along the wall. Durn: called down until he had no voice; there was a moan once, right after, then nothing — three days ago; no man lives at the bottom of a winze that long. Arris and Keld are gone. Floor test: the center of the floor sounds hollow; near the bend it's already gone (a ragged black mouth — the winze). Along the left wall the stone sounds truer and timbers stand closer, but the wood is old and powder-white, uncertain under his armored weight. The hole spans the middle of the gallery; Durn lies against the far wall just past the bend, on the other side. The pale light hangs over the winze mouth.
